nodeData.note: Organic production guides: maize, beans & grain legumes, rice, sugarcane, potato.

children.note: How to grow maize organically: varieties, soil and nutrition, water, pests, diseases, Striga, safe drying and storage, and markets — with Kenya and India notes.
How to grow common beans and other grain legumes — cowpea, pigeon pea, green gram and chickpea — organically, using nodule bacteria, healthy soil and natural pest control.
How to grow rice organically: SRI, Azolla and blue-green algae for nitrogen, water-saving irrigation, and biological control of blast, borers and hoppers, with Kenya (Mwea) and India notes.
How to grow sugarcane organically: clean bud-chip seed, press mud and legumes, Gluconacetobacter, trash mulching instead of burning, and ratoon care, with Kenya and India notes.

How to grow Irish potato organically, from clean seed to storage: climate, soil, organic nutrition with biofertilizers, water, the main pests and diseases with organic control, and markets in Kenya, India and beyond.

nodeData.note: How to grow maize organically: varieties, soil and nutrition, water, pests, diseases, Striga, safe drying and storage, and markets — with Kenya and India notes.

children.note: Maize (Zea mays) is a grass and the main staple cereal of East and Southern Africa, also a major food, feed and starch crop in India and worldwide.
Maize uses the efficient C4 photosynthesis pathway and is wind-pollinated: pollen from the tassel falls on the silks of the cob.

manas.q: How is maize pollinated?

children.note: Hybrid seed gives higher yields but must be bought new each season; saved seed of open-pollinated varieties (OPVs) stays true to type and can be replanted.

manas.q: Why can a farmer replant OPV maize seed but not hybrid seed?

children.note: KALRO and seed companies release varieties by zone: late highland hybrids (e.g. H614D), mid-altitude hybrids (e.g. H513) and early dryland types (e.g. DH04, Katumani Composite B, an OPV).
Most Indian maize is single-cross hybrid; ICAR has released quality-protein maize (QPM) and specialty types such as sweet corn and baby corn.
Public breeding (CIMMYT and national programmes) has released drought- and heat-tolerant maize for tropical rain-fed farms.
Genetically modified (e.g. Bt) maize is prohibited under all organic standards, so organic farmers need verified non-GM, untreated seed.

manas.q: Can Bt maize be grown on a certified organic farm?

children.note: Maize grows best in warm, sunny seasons with steady rain and deep, fertile, well-drained soil.
Maize is a warm-season crop that is killed by frost and grows slowly in cold highlands; very hot, dry winds at flowering cause poor seed set.
Late highland types need a long wet season; early types fit short rains or dry zones where the season may end early.
Deep, well-drained loams rich in organic matter suit it best; maize hates waterlogging and suffers on compacted or very acid soils.

manas.q: Name two soil conditions maize does not tolerate.

children.note: A slightly acid to neutral soil suits maize; on strongly acid soils (common in western Kenya) liming and organic matter improve yields.
Maize is direct-sown; good seedbed, timing and spacing set the yield before any input is applied.
Reduced tillage with crop residues on the surface keeps moisture and soil life; deep ploughing every season burns organic matter.
Early planting gives the most yield and lets the crop escape later stemborer and fall armyworm peaks.

manas.q: Why does early planting help maize against pests?

children.note: A common Kenyan recommendation is rows 75 cm apart with one seed every 25 cm (or two every 50 cm), sown about 5 cm deep.
Placing well-made compost or manure in the planting hole or furrow puts nutrients where young roots are.
Beans, cowpea, pigeon pea or desmodium between maize rows add nitrogen, cover soil and reduce pests and Striga.

links.label: 📄 Source: Pest Manag. Sci. 2021 (Desmodium, beans and FAW)

children.note: Maize is a heavy feeder, especially of nitrogen; organic plans build soil fertility over seasons rather than feeding only the crop.
Grain carries away most of the N and P; the stover holds much of the K, so returning stover or composting it saves potassium.

manas.q: Which part of the maize plant holds much of the potassium?

children.note: Yellowing starts at the tip of older, lower leaves and runs down the midrib in a V shape.

manas.q: What does nitrogen deficiency look like on maize leaves?

children.note: Well-made compost or farmyard manure at planting is the base; uncomposted manure can carry weeds and burn seedlings.
Rotations with legumes, mucuna or lablab cover crops, and Tithonia leaves (used in Kenya) supply nitrogen for the next maize.
Rapid growth before tasselling needs most nitrogen: side-dress compost, liquid manure or plant tea around knee height.
Living inputs that help maize take up nitrogen and phosphorus.
Coat seed with Azospirillum or Azotobacter plus PSB in a sticker just before sowing, in the shade.

manas.q: Which biofertilizers are used as seed treatment for maize?

children.note: Mix biofertilizers or Trichoderma with compost and apply in the furrow at planting so they colonise the roots.
Arbuscular mycorrhiza helps maize take up phosphorus and water; reduced tillage keeps the fungal network alive.
Azospirillum lives on cereal roots, fixes some nitrogen and boosts root hairs; it complements, not replaces, manure.
A 2022 study found nitrogen-fixing bacteria living in maize stem sap; still research, not a field product yet.
Most maize is rain-fed; the key is to keep water in the soil and protect the flowering stage.
Drought at tasselling and silking causes the biggest yield losses because silks dry out and grains do not set.

manas.q: At which growth stage is maize most sensitive to drought?

children.note: Zai pits, tied ridges and mulch catch rain where it falls and help maize in dry areas.
Standing water for a few days damages roots and causes yellowing; drain low spots or plant on ridges.
Caterpillars dominate in the field, weevils and the larger grain borer in store.
Ragged holes and wet sawdust-like frass in the whorl; larva has an inverted Y on the head and four dots near the tail.
Early planting, scouting, crushing egg masses and young larvae, Bt or neem sprays into the whorl, and natural enemies.
Climate-adapted push–pull with Desmodium and Brachiaria reduced fall armyworm damage in East African trials.
Full guide to fall armyworm, stemborers and other caterpillars.
Window panes and shot holes in leaves, 'dead heart' in young plants, tunnels in stems and broken tassels.
Push–pull, destroying or composting old stalks, early planting and the parasitic wasp Cotesia.

manas.q: How do old maize stalks help stemborers survive?

children.note: Cutworms cut seedlings at soil level at night; termites attack roots and lodged plants in dry spells.
Guide to cutworms, termites, white grubs and other soil pests.
Corn leaf aphids colonise tassels; leafhoppers spread maize streak virus.
Aphids, leafhoppers and thrips and their natural enemies.
Store pests that bore into grain and turn it to powder; the larger grain borer can destroy unshelled cobs fast.
Hermetic storage, drying and other organic storage methods.
Viruses, leaf blights, rusts and ear rots are the main maize diseases worldwide.
Two viruses together (MCMV plus a potyvirus such as SCMV); leaves yellow from the margins, then whole plants dry up and cobs are empty.
MLN was reported in Bomet, Kenya in 2011 and spread to neighbouring countries.

manas.q: Which two viruses together cause maize lethal necrosis?

children.note: Certified clean seed, tolerant varieties, no continuous maize (rotate with legumes), a maize-free break and removing sick plants.
How viruses spread and how to manage vectors organically.
Narrow broken yellow streaks along the veins; spread by Cicadulina leafhoppers, worst in late-planted crops.

manas.q: Which insect spreads maize streak virus?

children.note: Grey leaf spot gives long rectangular grey lesions limited by veins; northern leaf blight gives long cigar-shaped tan lesions.
Resistant varieties, rotation, burying or composting infected residues and wider spacing for air flow.
Leaf blights, their look-alikes and organic control.
Rust gives brick-red powdery pustules on both leaf surfaces; downy mildew (important in India) gives pale streaks and white growth.
Recognising and managing mildews and rusts.
Pink, white, green or grey mould on cobs; Aspergillus flavus can make aflatoxin, a poison you cannot see.
Aflatoxin-contaminated maize caused deadly acute poisoning outbreaks in Kenya in 2004–2005.

manas.q: Why is mouldy maize dangerous even after cooking?

children.note: Spreading native non-toxic Aspergillus flavus strains in the field crowds out toxic ones; products are registered in several African countries.
Avoid drought stress, control insects that damage cobs, harvest on time and don't leave cobs in wet fields.
Weeds compete hardest in the first weeks; parasitic Striga is the most damaging weed of African maize.
Keep maize clean for roughly the first 4–6 weeks; later weeds cost less yield.

manas.q: When must maize be kept weed-free?

children.note: A purple-flowered parasite attached to maize roots; the maize stunts and wilts before Striga even emerges.
Root exudates of Desmodium intercrops trigger Striga seeds to germinate and stop them attaching, depleting the seed bank.

manas.q: How does Desmodium reduce Striga?

children.note: Pull Striga before it seeds, add manure, rotate with trap crops like cowpea or soybean, and use tolerant varieties.
Weed ecology and organic weed control.
Residue mulch and legume intercrops shade out weeds and protect soil between weedings.
Most aflatoxin and insect damage happens after harvest, so drying and storage decide grain quality.
Grain is mature when a black layer forms at the base of the kernel; then dry it in the field or on racks.

manas.q: What sign shows maize grain is physiologically mature?

children.note: Dry cobs on tarpaulins, raised racks or cribs; soil contact spreads Aspergillus and re-wets grain.
Shelled grain should be dry enough to rattle and crack between the teeth; moisture meters are more reliable.
Remove mouldy, insect-damaged and shrivelled cobs and grain; they carry most of the toxin.
Airtight bags or metal silos starve insects of oxygen and keep grain safe without chemicals.

manas.q: How do hermetic bags kill storage insects?

children.note: Organic maize is mostly sold locally or as feed; the premium depends on clean grain and good records.
East African and EU standards set strict maximum aflatoxin levels; mouldy grain can be rejected or destroyed.
Organic poultry and dairy farms need certified maize, making feed a key outlet.
Kenya exports baby corn and sweet corn to Europe as vegetables; residues and quality rules apply as for other fresh produce.
Use non-GM untreated seed, keep a buffer from GM or sprayed fields, record inputs and follow your standard.
Short videos from research and extension organisations.
How Desmodium and Brachiaria control Striga and stemborers in maize.
CIMMYT on MLN symptoms, spread and how farmers can prevent it.
University of Nebraska shows how to identify grey leaf spot lesions.
Doubling over mature stalks so cobs dry in the field and shed rain.
How to dry and store maize to avoid aflatoxin.
Simple steps for clean, dry, pest-free maize storage.
Reliable sources for deeper study.
Manuals and evidence on push–pull for stemborers, Striga and fall armyworm.
Review of the MLN outbreak, its viruses and management.
FAO guidance on monitoring and managing fall armyworm.
Free Kenyan site on organic and ecological crop production and pest control.
Background on maize biology, history and uses.

nodeData.note: How to grow common beans and other grain legumes — cowpea, pigeon pea, green gram and chickpea — organically, using nodule bacteria, healthy soil and natural pest control.

children.note: Grain legumes (pulses) feed people with protein and feed the soil with nitrogen fixed by root-nodule bacteria.
Phaseolus vulgaris, grown as dry beans and as green French beans; the most eaten grain legume in East Africa.
Bush types mature fast; climbing beans need stakes but can yield much more on small plots, popular in Rwanda and western Kenya.

manas.q: Why do farmers on small plots grow climbing beans?

children.note: KALRO releases include Rosecoco and Mwitemania types for the highlands, KAT B1 and KAT B9 for dry areas, and iron-rich Nyota.
Vigna unguiculata: the most drought- and heat-tolerant pulse; leaves are eaten as a vegetable and grain is dried.

manas.q: Which grain legume tolerates the most heat and drought?

links.label: 📄 Source: Front. Plant Sci. 2016 (cowpea in Africa)

children.note: Cajanus cajan: a deep-rooted shrubby legume grown in dry eastern Kenya and across India (tur/arhar), often intercropped with maize or sorghum.
Vigna radiata (mung bean, ndengu): a fast, short-season pulse for dry lowlands; Kenya grows it widely in Eastern region.
Cicer arietinum: India's biggest pulse, grown in the cool dry season on stored soil moisture; also grown on black cotton soils in Kenya.

manas.q: When is chickpea grown in India?

children.note: Each pulse has its own niche; all hate waterlogging and acid, poor soils limit nodulation.
It grows best in mild mid-altitude climates; heat and drought at flowering cause flower and pod drop.
Cowpea, green gram and pigeon pea suit hot, drier lowlands; chickpea suits cool, dry seasons.
Well-drained loams with good organic matter; waterlogged soils rot roots and kill nodules.

manas.q: Why are legumes poor on waterlogged soils?

children.note: Very acid soils hurt both the plant and its rhizobia; liming and manure help beans on acid Kenyan highland soils.

links.label: 📄 Source: Microbiol. Mol. Biol. Rev. 1999 (rhizobia under stress)

children.note: Clean seed, good spacing and the right partner crops give a healthy stand.
Many bean diseases (anthracnose, blights, BCMV) are seed-borne: use certified or carefully selected seed from healthy plants.

manas.q: Why does clean seed matter so much for beans?

children.note: Bush beans are commonly sown about 45–50 cm between rows and 10–15 cm within the row; pigeon pea needs much wider spacing.
Beans or cowpea between maize rows give two crops, fix nitrogen and can reduce fall armyworm on the maize.

links.label: 📄 Source: Pest Manag. Sci. 2021 (Desmodium, beans and FAW)

children.note: Do not plant beans after beans; rotating with cereals breaks root rot and disease cycles.
Legumes make most of their own nitrogen if well nodulated, but they still need phosphorus, potassium and micronutrients.

children.topic: Common bean is a weak fixer
children.note: Common bean fixes less nitrogen than cowpea, soybean or pigeon pea, so it responds to compost and good nodulation.
Nodules need lots of P and energy; P shortage is the most common limit to N fixation on African soils.

manas.q: Which nutrient most often limits nitrogen fixation in legumes?

links.label: 📄 Source: Microbiol. Mol. Biol. Rev. 1999 (rhizobia under stress)

children.note: Molybdenum is part of the nitrogenase enzyme; Ca and S also support nodules. Acid soils often lack Mo.
Apply well-made compost in the furrow at planting; too much fresh nitrogen reduces nodulation.
In one study biochar raised the share of nitrogen beans fixed from the air.

links.label: 📄 Source: Biol. Fertil. Soils 2007 (biochar and bean BNF)

children.note: Living inputs for pulses, applied mostly on the seed.
Coat seed with the right Rhizobium in a sugar or gum sticker, in the shade, and sow the same day.

manas.q: How long can inoculated seed wait before sowing?

children.topic: Match the strain to the crop
children.note: Each pulse needs its own group: Rhizobium for common bean, Bradyrhizobium for cowpea, green gram and pigeon pea, Mesorhizobium for chickpea.

manas.q: Which rhizobium group nodulates chickpea?

children.note: Cowpea often nodulates with native soil bacteria, so it responds less to inoculation than common bean or soybean.
PSB with rhizobium improves P supply; Trichoderma seed treatment protects against root rots — apply it first, then rhizobium.
Dig up a plant: active nodules are pink to red inside; white, green or no nodules mean poor fixation.

manas.q: What colour are active nodules inside?

children.note: Pulses use less water than cereals but suffer at flowering and pod fill.
Flowering and pod filling are the most sensitive stages; stress then drops flowers and leaves pods empty.

manas.q: When are beans most sensitive to drought?

children.note: Mulch and tied ridges keep moisture; avoid overhead watering late in the day, which favours leaf diseases.
Plant on raised beds in wet areas; even short waterlogging invites root rots.
Bean fly and aphids attack early; pod borers attack flowers and pods; bruchids attack in store.
Ophiomyia flies lay eggs in leaves; maggots tunnel to the stem base, which swells and cracks, and seedlings wilt and die.
Plant early, earth up soil around stems to promote new roots, mulch, keep plants vigorous with compost, and grow tolerant varieties.

manas.q: How does earthing up help beans against bean fly?

children.note: Soil and stem-base pests and how to manage them.
Black aphids on shoots and pods spread bean common mosaic virus; thrips scar flowers and cause flower drop.
Aphids, thrips, whiteflies and their natural enemies.
Larvae web flowers, pods and leaves together and bore into pods; a major pest of cowpea and pigeon pea.
Parasitic wasps (e.g. Apanteles taragamae introduced in Benin), neem and Bt sprays at flowering.

links.label: 📄 Source: J. Chem. Ecol. 2010 (Apanteles vs Maruca)

children.note: Green to brown larvae make round holes in pods of chickpea and pigeon pea and eat the seeds.
Pheromone traps, bird perches, hand shaking of pigeon pea plants onto sheets, HearNPV and neem sprays.

manas.q: Name a specific virus product for Helicoverpa.

children.note: Caterpillar biology and organic control in detail.
Ootheca and other beetles chew round holes in leaves of young beans and cowpea.
Beetle pests and organic control.
Small beetles lay eggs on seeds; larvae eat inside and adults leave round exit holes.
Hermetic storage and other organic store protection.
Many bean diseases ride on seed and splash with rain, so clean seed and dry foliage are the first defence.
Angular leaf spot: brown angular spots boxed in by veins. Anthracnose: dark sunken pod lesions and blackened veins under leaves.
Clean seed, resistant varieties, rotation, removing debris and staying out of the field when leaves are wet.

manas.q: Why stay out of a bean field when leaves are wet?

children.note: Fungal leaf and pod blights in detail.
Common blight: brown leaf patches with yellow edges. Halo blight: small spots with a wide yellow halo; both seed-borne.
Bacterial diseases and organic options, including copper limits.
Rust gives rusty-brown powdery pustules under leaves; powdery mildew (common in green gram) gives white dusty patches.
Recognition and organic control of mildews and rusts.
Fusarium, Pythium and Rhizoctonia rot the roots: plants yellow, stunt and die in patches, worst on tired, wet soils.
Rotation, raised beds, compost, Trichoderma seed treatment and tolerant climbing varieties.
Root rot pathogens and soil-health solutions.
Chickpea and pigeon pea wilt: plants droop and dry while the inner stem shows brown streaks.
Wilt diseases and how to tell them apart.
BCMV (bean mosaic, aphid- and seed-borne), yellow mosaic of green gram (whiteflies, India) and pigeon pea sterility mosaic (mites).

manas.q: Which vector spreads yellow mosaic of green gram?

children.note: Viruses, their vectors and prevention.
Pulses are short and grow slowly at first, so early weed control is vital.
Two weedings in the first four to six weeks usually protect most of the yield.
Working among wet bean plants spreads bacterial blights and anthracnose.
Striga gesnerioides and Alectra attack cowpea roots in dry Africa; use resistant varieties and rotation.

manas.q: Which parasitic weeds attack cowpea?

children.note: Timely harvest and dry storage protect grain from shattering, mould and bruchids.
Harvest when most pods are dry and yellow-brown; pigeon pea and cowpea are often picked in several rounds.
Dry plants on tarpaulins, thresh by beating gently in bags, then dry grain until it is hard.
Airtight triple-layer bags or sealed drums kill bruchids by cutting off oxygen, without chemicals.

manas.q: Why do airtight bags stop bruchids?

children.note: Coating seed with vegetable oil, mixing with ash, or using aromatic plants like basil can deter bruchids.

links.label: 📄 Source: J. Stored Prod. Res. 2001 (basil oils vs bruchids)

children.note: Heating grain in the sun under clear plastic kills bruchid eggs and larvae inside cowpea seeds.
Pulses sell well locally; French beans are a major Kenyan export with strict rules.
Kenya exports fresh green beans to Europe; buyers demand GLOBALG.A.P., traceability and KEPHIS inspection.
EU limits are very low; consignments with residues are rejected, so organic and biological control is a market advantage.

manas.q: Why do EU MRLs favour biological pest control?

children.note: India is the largest pulse producer and consumer, so tur, moong and chana have strong local demand.
Organic needs untreated seed and approved inoculants; chemical seed dressings are not allowed.
Short videos from research and extension organisations.
How to stake climbing beans for higher yields on small plots.
Natural ways to control aphids in beans and vegetables.
Step-by-step seed inoculation with rhizobium before sowing.
Animation on natural enemies and biopesticides for Maruca in cowpea.
Farmer video on controlling Helicoverpa pod borer in pigeon pea.
How to use airtight bags to keep bruchids out of stored pulses.
Reliable sources for deeper study.
Project resources on inoculating and growing legumes in Africa.
Free Kenyan site on organic pulse production and pest control.
Review of cowpea's role, constraints and breeding in sub-Saharan Africa.
Background on the common bean's biology and types.
Background on pigeon pea biology and uses.

nodeData.note: How to grow rice organically: SRI, Azolla and blue-green algae for nitrogen, water-saving irrigation, and biological control of blast, borers and hoppers, with Kenya (Mwea) and India notes.

children.note: Rice (Oryza sativa, plus African rice O. glaberrima) is a grass grown mostly in flooded paddies, but also in rainfed lowlands and uplands. It feeds more than half of the world.
Asian rice (Oryza sativa, with indica and japonica groups) dominates worldwide; African rice (O. glaberrima) was domesticated in West Africa and is hardier but lower yielding.

manas.q: Which two rice species are cultivated?

children.note: Irrigated lowland (most production), rainfed lowland, upland (dry fields, no flooding) and deep-water rice. Organic methods differ mainly in how water and weeds are handled.
Kenyan consumers pay a premium for aromatic Basmati, locally called Pishori, grown mainly under irrigation at Mwea. Non-aromatic types such as IR-lines are grown for yield.

manas.q: What do Kenyans call locally grown aromatic Basmati rice?

children.note: KALRO and partners have released higher-yielding, blast-tolerant lines (e.g. Komboka). Ask the scheme office or KALRO Mwea for seed suited to your block.
Widely grown examples include Swarna and Samba Mahsuri (non-aromatic) and Pusa Basmati types for export. State universities list varieties for each season and zone.
Prefer varieties with good blast and bacterial blight tolerance, strong roots and good tillering. Very high-input hybrids often disappoint without synthetic N.

manas.q: Which disease tolerances matter most when choosing an organic rice variety?

children.note: Rice is a warm-season crop that needs plenty of water. It tolerates flooding because its roots and stems carry air down through hollow tissue (aerenchyma).
Grows best in warm weather; cold nights at flowering cause empty grains, and very hot spells at flowering also reduce seed set.
Air channels (aerenchyma) carry oxygen from leaves to roots, so rice survives waterlogged soil that kills most crops.

manas.q: How do rice roots get oxygen in flooded soil?

children.note: Clay and clay-loam soils that hold water are ideal for paddies. Flooding brings soil pH towards neutral and makes P and iron more available.

Kenya's main rice area: the Mwea irrigation scheme in Kirinyaga County, started in 1954, fed by the Thiba river from Mount Kenya on heavy clay plains. Ahero and West Kano near Kisumu are other schemes.

manas.q: When was the Mwea irrigation scheme founded and which river feeds it?

links.label: 📄 Source: Wikipedia – Rice farming in Kenya

children.note: Good levelling and a healthy nursery are the foundation of organic rice; weak seedlings cannot outgrow weeds and pests.
A level field lets a shallow water layer cover all the soil evenly, so weeds are suppressed and water use falls.

manas.q: Why does field levelling matter so much in rice?

children.note: Ploughing in standing water makes a soft mud that holds water and buries weeds. Repeated puddling can damage soil structure for the next dry-season crop.
Float seed in salt water (a fresh egg should float); discard the light seeds that float and rinse the heavy ones. Heavy seed gives stronger seedlings.

manas.q: How do you separate heavy rice seed for sowing?

children.note: Treat soaked seed with Pseudomonas fluorescens or Trichoderma and Azospirillum/PSB before sowing in the nursery. Do not mix with chemical fungicides.
A well-drained nursery bed rich in compost gives sturdy seedlings. In SRI a small, mat-type nursery near the field is used.
Plant seedlings shallowly at even spacing in rows so a weeder can pass. Older seedlings recover more slowly from transplanting.
Seed can be broadcast or drilled into wet or dry soil, saving labour, but weeds become the main challenge in organic systems.
A set of practices developed in Madagascar by Fr. Henri de Laulanié: young single seedlings, wide spacing, moist not flooded soil, active weeding and organic matter.
Developed in Madagascar in the 1980s by the Jesuit priest Henri de Laulanié and later spread worldwide with support from Cornell University.

manas.q: Who developed SRI and where?

links.label: 📄 Source: Wikipedia – System of Rice Intensification

children.note: Transplant very young seedlings (around two leaves, often 8–12 days old), one per hill, gently and quickly so roots are not damaged.

manas.q: How old and how many seedlings per hill in SRI?

links.label: 📄 Source: Wikipedia – System of Rice Intensification

children.note: Wide spacing (often 25 × 25 cm or more) gives each plant room for roots and tillers and lets a weeder pass both ways.
Keep soil moist with intermittent irrigation instead of standing water during the vegetative stage, so roots get air and grow deeper.
A rotary or cono weeder is pushed between rows every 10–12 days; it kills weeds and aerates the soil. Weeds are returned as green manure.
Compost, manure and green manures feed the soil life that SRI depends on.
Aerated SRI soils favour beneficial root microbes; a review links much of the SRI benefit to the root microbiome.
Very high early yield claims were challenged by scientists; gains vary by site and skill. Water and seed savings are more consistent than yield records.
Feed the soil before planting, add biological N from Azolla, algae and bacteria during the crop, and recycle straw.
Most nitrogen and phosphorus leave in the grain, while most potassium and silicon stay in the straw. Returning straw recycles much of the K.

manas.q: Which nutrients stay mostly in rice straw?

children.note: Apply well-made compost or farmyard manure before final puddling so it is mixed into the mud.
Grow dhaincha (Sesbania) or sunn hemp for 6–8 weeks and plough it in before transplanting; it adds N and organic matter.

manas.q: Name two green manures ploughed in before rice.

children.note: Azolla is a floating fern that hosts the N-fixing cyanobacterium Anabaena. Grown in the paddy water alongside rice, it fixes nitrogen and is later trampled into the soil.

manas.q: Which cyanobacterium lives inside Azolla?

children.note: Besides N, an Azolla cover shades the water, suppresses weeds and keeps water pH from rising, which reduces ammonia loss.

links.label: 📄 Source: Biol Fertil Soils 1999 (BGA & Azolla review)

children.note: Blue-green algae (cyanobacteria such as Nostoc, Anabaena) are spread as soil-based flakes into the standing water after transplanting; they fix N in the flood water.

manas.q: What is algalization in rice?

children.note: Dip seedling roots in a slurry of Azospirillum and phosphate-solubilizing bacteria before transplanting.
Zinc deficiency (bronze, stunted seedlings; "khaira" in India) is common in flooded alkaline soils. Organic standards allow zinc salts only when deficiency is shown.
Rice takes up a lot of silicon, which stiffens leaves against blast and insects. Straw, husk ash and compost return silicon and K.
Rice uses more water than other crops, but continuous deep flooding is not needed for good yields.
Water shortage hurts most at panicle initiation and flowering. Drain about 1–2 weeks before harvest.
Let the field water drop below the surface, then re-flood. A perforated pipe (field water tube) shows the water level in the soil.

manas.q: What tool shows when to re-irrigate in AWD?

children.note: A meta-analysis found no significant yield loss when water was allowed to drop only to about 15 cm below the surface, with about 23% less water; severe drying cut yields by about 23%.

manas.q: How far can water drop in "safe" AWD?

children.note: AWD roughly halved methane emissions in a global meta-analysis, though nitrous oxide rose somewhat.

links.label: 📄 Source: Global Change Biology 2024 (AWD emissions meta-analysis)

children.note: Without standing water, weeds grow faster, so AWD and SRI need timely mechanical weeding.
Healthy, unsprayed paddies hold many spiders, dragonflies and parasitoids that keep most pests below damaging levels.
Yellow stem borer (Asia) and African stem borers (e.g. Maliarpha, Chilo) tunnel in stems.
Young plants show "deadhearts" (central shoot dries and pulls out); at heading, "whiteheads" are empty white panicles that stand upright.

manas.q: What are deadhearts and whiteheads in rice?

children.note: Collect egg masses from seedbeds, clip seedling leaf tips before transplanting, release Trichogramma egg parasitoid cards, cut stubble low after harvest.
Borers, armyworms and their organic control in detail.
Cnaphalocrocis caterpillars fold leaves lengthwise and scrape the green tissue, leaving white streaks. Usually controlled by natural enemies; avoid early sprays.
Nilaparvata lugens sucks sap at the plant base; patches dry out suddenly ("hopperburn"). Outbreaks follow excess N and insecticide sprays that kill spiders.

manas.q: Which two practices trigger brown planthopper outbreaks?

children.note: Balanced organic N, alleyways every few metres for air, draining the field for a few days, and conserving spiders and mirid predators.
Hoppers, bugs and aphids in detail.
Larvae turn the growing shoot into a hollow tube, the "onion leaf" or silver shoot. Use tolerant varieties and avoid staggered planting.
Rice bugs suck milky grains, leaving empty or spotted grain. Birds such as quelea in Africa raid ripening fields; synchronous planting and scaring help.
Most rice diseases are managed by resistant varieties, clean seed, balanced nutrition and good spacing.
Caused by the fungus Magnaporthe oryzae (Pyricularia). The most important rice disease worldwide.
Spindle- or eye-shaped leaf spots with grey centres and brown edges; "neck blast" rots the panicle neck so grains stay empty.

manas.q: Describe a rice blast leaf lesion.

children.note: High N, long leaf wetness, cool nights with dew, and dry-nursery or upland conditions.
Resistant varieties, moderate N, silicon from straw and husk ash, seed treatment and sprays with Pseudomonas fluorescens or Bacillus.
Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzae: yellow stripes with wavy edges from the leaf tip down; young plants may wilt ("kresek"). Spreads with water and wind-driven rain.

manas.q: What does bacterial leaf blight look like on rice?

children.note: Rhizoctonia solani makes oval grey-green lesions with brown borders on the sheath near the water line, like snake skin. Wider spacing and less N help.
Bipolaris oryzae: small round brown spots. It is a sign of poor, nutrient-starved soils, especially low K and silicon.
An African virus first reported in Kenya in 1966: yellow-mottled leaves and stunting. Spread by beetles and by contact; use tolerant varieties and remove ratoons.

manas.q: Where was rice yellow mottle virus first reported?

children.note: Synthetic fungicides such as tricyclazole are not allowed in organic rice. Copper is allowed only within certifier limits.
General disease biology and organic control.
How bacterial diseases spread and are managed.
Weeds are the biggest yield limit in organic rice, especially without standing water.
A shallow, continuous water layer after transplanting stops most grass weeds from germinating.
Pushed between rows 2–4 times in the first 40 days; they bury weeds and aerate soil.

manas.q: When are rotary weeders used in rice?

children.note: Flood and prepare the land, let weeds sprout, then kill them with the final puddling before planting.
Rice-duck (aigamo) and rice-fish systems in Asia use animals to eat weeds and insects while adding manure.
Red or weedy rice looks like crop rice but shatters early. Use clean certified seed and transplant rather than broadcast.
Principles and tools for weed control.
Good timing and fast drying protect yield and quality, especially for premium aromatic rice.
Harvest when most grains (about 80–85%) are straw-coloured and hard. Late harvest causes shattering and cracked grains.
Dry paddy quickly to about 14% moisture for safe storage; slow or uneven drying causes mould and broken rice in milling.

manas.q: To what moisture content should paddy be dried for storage?

children.note: Airtight bags or silos starve insects of oxygen, an organic-allowed method against weevils and moths.
Rice weevil, grain moth and organic storage methods.
Return straw as mulch or compost instead of burning; burning wastes K and silicon and pollutes the air.
Organic rice earns more where buyers trust the label, mainly aromatic types.
Kenya produces far less rice than it eats and imports mainly from India and Pakistan, so local aromatic rice has a ready market.

links.label: 📄 Source: Wikipedia – Rice farming in Kenya

children.note: India exports organic Basmati under NPOP certification; EU buyers test strictly for pesticide residues such as tricyclazole.

manas.q: Which fungicide residue has caused problems for Basmati exports to the EU?

children.note: Paddies share water, so a certified field needs protection from neighbours' sprayed water: own inlet, buffer strip, records.
AWD reduces methane, and some carbon programmes pay rice farmers for verified water-saving practices.
Standards, PGS and group certification.
Videos on SRI, transplanting and Kenyan rice.
FAO short film on the principles and benefits of SRI.
ECHO Asia walks through SRI nursery, spacing and weeding.
A longer training film showing SRI steps in farmers' fields.
Farmer-to-farmer video on careful transplanting in rows.
Kenyan TV report on how Mwea rice farming began and works.
IRRI introduces its app for diagnosing rice pests and diseases.
Trusted sources for organic rice.
Practical guides on every stage of rice production.
SRI principles, country reports and research.
Organic pest and crop guides for East Africa.
Indian rice package of practices, biofertilizers and organic methods.

nodeData.note: How to grow sugarcane organically: clean bud-chip seed, press mud and legumes, Gluconacetobacter, trash mulching instead of burning, and ratoon care, with Kenya and India notes.

children.note: Sugarcane is a tall perennial C4 grass grown for sugar, jaggery and ethanol. One planting gives a plant crop and then several ratoon crops from the stubble.
Commercial canes are hybrids of noble cane (Saccharum officinarum) with wild S. spontaneum, which added vigour, hardiness and disease resistance.

manas.q: Which two Saccharum species are behind modern cane hybrids?

children.note: A plant crop takes roughly 10–18 months to mature depending on climate; ratoons are usually a little faster.
Most Indian varieties carry the "Co" prefix from the Sugarcane Breeding Institute, Coimbatore (e.g. Co 0238 in the north, Co 86032 in the south).

manas.q: What does the "Co" in Indian cane variety names refer to?

children.note: Grown mainly in western Kenya and the Lake Victoria basin by outgrowers supplying mills. Varieties come from the KALRO Sugar Research Institute at Kibos.
Pick varieties with red rot and smut resistance, good ratooning ability and early vigour to shade out weeds.
Cane needs a long warm, sunny growing season with plenty of water, then a cooler or drier ripening period.
Growth is fastest in hot, humid weather; frost damages cane and cold slows it.
A cool or dry spell before harvest slows growth and lets the plant store more sucrose in the stalk.

manas.q: What weather helps cane store more sugar before harvest?

children.note: Deep, well-drained loams with good organic matter are best. Waterlogging, hard pans and salinity reduce rooting and yield.
Continuous cane with burning and heavy machinery runs down soil carbon and structure; organic systems rebuild it with trash, legumes and compost.
Healthy seed cane and deep, well-prepared furrows set up the whole crop cycle, including the ratoons.
Break any hard pan and plant in furrows or trenches so roots go deep and later earthing up is easy.
Take setts from a young (about 8–10 month) disease-free seed nursery; most cane diseases travel in infected setts.

manas.q: Why is clean seed cane so important?

children.note: Treating setts in hot water (or aerated steam) before planting reduces ratoon stunting and grassy shoot; it needs accurate temperature control.
Soak setts in a slurry of Trichoderma plus Gluconacetobacter or Azospirillum and PSB before planting. Do not mix with chemical fungicides.
Single buds are raised as seedlings in trays and transplanted at about a month old. This saves a lot of seed cane and gives even stands.

manas.q: What is the main saving of bud-chip planting?

children.note: The Sustainable Sugarcane Initiative in India combines bud-chip seedlings, wide spacing, organic matter and water saving, similar to SRI in rice.
Wide or paired rows allow legumes or vegetables between the rows in the first 3–4 months and later machine work.
Cane is a heavy feeder, especially of N and K, so organic growers combine bulky manures, mill by-products, legumes and biofertilizers.
Large amounts of K and N leave in harvested stalks; leaves and tops (trash) hold much of the K, so keeping trash in the field matters.
A mill by-product rich in organic matter, phosphorus and calcium. Compost it before use; fresh press mud can heat up and attract pests.

manas.q: Which nutrient is press mud especially rich in?

children.note: Apply compost or farmyard manure in the furrows at planting and after each ratoon harvest.
Sunn hemp or dhaincha ploughed in before planting, or cowpea, beans and soybean between rows, add N and protect soil.
Distillery effluent (vinasse) is rich in K but must be treated and applied under rules; check if your organic certifier accepts it.
Gluconacetobacter diazotrophicus is an N-fixing bacterium that lives inside cane stems, roots and leaves. It was found in Brazil by Cavalcante and Döbereiner.

manas.q: Where inside the plant does Gluconacetobacter live?

children.note: Its contribution varies strongly between cane varieties and sites, so treat it as a supplement to manure, not a full replacement.
Besides N, it makes growth hormones (auxins); in studies it improved drought tolerance of cane.
Apply phosphate-solubilizing and potash-mobilizing bacteria with compost in furrows; mycorrhiza helps root uptake of P.
Spreading the dry leaves (trash) on the field instead of burning them is the single biggest soil-building practice in cane.
Burning wastes N, K and organic matter, kills soil life and natural enemies, and pollutes the air.

manas.q: Name two losses caused by burning cane trash.

children.note: Spread trash between rows (often alternate rows) after harvest; sprinkle with cow-dung slurry or a decomposer culture to speed breakdown.
Conserves soil moisture, smothers weeds, cools the soil, feeds earthworms and returns potassium.

manas.q: List three benefits of trash mulching.

children.note: Brazilian field trials found total or high straw removal harmed soil health, especially on sandy soils; low or moderate removal had little short-term effect.
Remove and compost trash from fields with heavy disease or pest attack; keep trash away from cane rows in frost or fire-risk areas.
Cane needs a lot of water, most of all during tillering and the grand growth phase.
Tillering and grand growth (fast stalk elongation) are most sensitive to water stress; stress then reduces cane weight sharply.

manas.q: Which growth phases of cane are most sensitive to drought?

children.note: Drip saves water and can deliver filtered liquid manures and biofertilizers (fertigation) to the root zone.
Irrigating alternate furrows and keeping a trash mulch cut water use.
Reduce irrigation in the weeks before harvest to raise sugar content.
Ratoons regrow from the stubble after harvest, saving planting costs, but yield declines with each ratoon unless managed well.
The new crop of shoots that sprouts from underground buds of the harvested stubble.

manas.q: What is a sugarcane ratoon?

children.note: Cut stubble level with the ground so new shoots come from deep, strong buds.
Loosen soil on the row sides, then apply compost, press mud and biofertilizers soon after harvest.
Fill gaps in the row with bud-chip seedlings within a few weeks so the stand stays full.
Yields fall over ratoons due to soil compaction, pests, diseases and variety; good care slows the decline.
Replant when gaps, disease (smut, ratoon stunting) or yield decline make the ratoon unprofitable.
Borers, white grubs, termites and sucking pests are the main cane pests; parasitoid releases and healthy soil are the organic backbone.
Chilo infuscatellus attacks young cane in the first months.
Central shoot dries (deadheart) and pulls out easily with a foul smell; small holes near the base.

manas.q: How do you recognize early shoot borer damage?

children.note: Early trash mulching, earthing up, removing deadhearts and Trichogramma chilonis egg-parasitoid releases.
Larvae bore into internodes or the top shoot; top borer causes a "bunchy top". Trichogramma releases and removing egg masses help.
Eldana saccharina, the African stalk borer, tunnels stalks in East and southern Africa; older and water-stressed cane suffers most.
Borers, Trichogramma and biological control.
Grubs and termites eat roots and setts; cane yellows and topples. Use Metarhizium/Beauveria with compost and avoid raw manure.

manas.q: Which fungi are used against white grubs?

children.note: Grubs, termites and soil-pest biocontrol.
Woolly aphid covers leaves in white wax; pyrilla leafhoppers suck sap. Both are often held down by predators and parasitoids when not sprayed.
Aphids, hoppers and their natural enemies.
Most cane diseases come in with infected setts, so clean seed and resistant varieties are the first defence.
Caused by Colletotrichum falcatum, mainly in South Asia.
Upper leaves dry; a split stalk shows red tissue with white cross-bands and a sour, alcohol smell.

manas.q: What does a split stalk with red rot look like?

children.note: Resistant varieties, healthy setts, crop rotation, field drainage and Trichoderma with compost; destroy infected clumps.

links.label: 📄 Source: Plant Physiol Biochem 2020 (Bacillus vs red rot)

children.note: Sporisorium scitamineum: a black whip grows from the shoot tip. Bag and remove whips before they burst; use resistant varieties and clean setts.

manas.q: What is the typical sign of sugarcane smut?

children.note: A bacterium (Leifsonia xyli) clogs the vessels; ratoons are stunted with no clear outward sign. Spread by cutting knives; disinfect tools and use hot-water-treated seed.

manas.q: How does ratoon stunting disease spread between fields?

children.note: A phytoplasma causes many thin, pale grass-like shoots; spread by setts and leafhoppers. Rogue affected clumps.
Xanthomonas albilineans makes white pencil-line stripes on leaves; lab work shows Gluconacetobacter can inhibit it.
Wilts and vascular diseases in detail.
Cane rusts and other leaf diseases.
Weeds compete hardest in the first 3–4 months before the cane canopy closes.
Keep the field clean in the early months; later the canopy shades weeds out.

manas.q: When is weed control most critical in cane?

children.note: Legume intercrops and trash mulch cover the soil and suppress weeds while adding N and organic matter.
Hoeing and earthing up between rows control weeds and support the stalks.
Principles and tools for weed control.
Harvest at peak sugar and crush quickly; sugar is lost every hour cut cane waits.
A hand refractometer measures juice brix; when top and bottom brix are nearly equal the cane is ripe.

manas.q: How can a farmer check cane ripeness in the field?

children.note: Cut close to the ground (sugar is richest at the base) and deliver to the mill quickly; delays reduce weight and sugar recovery.
Organic and green-cane harvesting keeps trash for mulch and avoids sugar losses from burnt cane.
Organic jaggery (gur), cane syrup and fresh juice earn premiums; hygiene and no chemical clarifiers are needed for organic.
Most cane goes to mills, so organic cane needs a mill or jaggery unit willing to process it separately.
Smallholders supply cane to mills under contract; organic cane needs a buyer that keeps it separate. Jaggery units offer another outlet.
The central government sets a fair and remunerative price (FRP) for cane each season; organic jaggery and sugar sell above it.
Organic sugar or jaggery needs certified fields plus a certified, segregated processing line (NPOP in India, EU/US standards for export).
Brazil is a leading supplier of organic sugar; buyers in the EU and US test residues and want full traceability.
Videos on bud-chip planting, trash mulching, ratoons and borers.
Solidaridad India explains the benefits of mulching cane trash.
Indian national extension institute on caring for ratoon crops.
UP Council of Sugarcane Research training on raising bud seedlings.
Telangana agricultural university demonstrates bud-chip planting.
Recognizing early shoot borer damage in young cane.
Queensland Agriculture on soil health and yield in cane fields.
Trusted sources for organic sugarcane.
Varieties, bud-chip technology and pest guides from Coimbatore.
Sugarcane production technology for subtropical India.
Indian package of practices, trash mulching and biofertilizers for cane.
Organic crop and pest guides for East Africa.

nodeData.note: How to grow Irish potato organically, from clean seed to storage: climate, soil, organic nutrition with biofertilizers, water, the main pests and diseases with organic control, and markets in Kenya, India and beyond.

children.note: Potato is the world's most important non-grain food crop and a major cash crop in the Kenyan highlands and the Indian plains and hills.
A member of the nightshade family (Solanaceae) with tomato, eggplant and peppers. It was domesticated in the Andes of South America.

manas.q: Which plant family does potato belong to?

children.topic: A tuber is a swollen stem
children.note: The tuber forms at the tip of underground stems called stolons. Its eyes are buds, which is why a tuber can be planted as seed.

manas.q: Is a potato tuber a root or a stem?

children.note: Seed potatoes are grown and kept for planting; ware potatoes are sold for eating or processing. Seed needs much stricter disease control.
Fresh tubers will not sprout for weeks to months (dormancy, which differs by variety). Plant tubers with short, sturdy, green sprouts for a fast, even stand.

manas.q: What kind of sprouts should a seed tuber have at planting?

children.note: Shangi is the most widely grown (short dormancy, popular in markets, but blight-susceptible). Others include Dutch Robjyn, Unica, Sherekea and processing types such as Markies; check KALRO/KEPHIS lists.
ICAR-CPRI (Shimla) has bred the Kufri series, e.g. Kufri Jyoti, Kufri Pukhraj, Kufri Bahar and processing types such as Kufri Chipsona.
A cool-season crop: it grows best in mild days and cool nights on deep, loose, well-drained soil.
Tubers set and bulk best in mild weather; hot nights push growth into leaves and cut tuber formation. Frost kills the foliage.

manas.q: Why do hot nights reduce potato yields?

children.note: In Kenya it is a highland crop (roughly 1,500–3,000 m) grown in both rainy seasons. In India it is mainly a rabi (winter) crop in the plains and a summer crop in the hills.
Tubers need soft soil to swell evenly; heavy or compacted clay gives small, misshapen tubers and rots in waterlogged spots.
Potato tolerates acid soil (around pH 5–6.5). Raising pH with heavy liming favours common scab, so lime only if a soil test shows a real need.

manas.q: Why should you avoid heavy liming before potatoes?

children.note: Do not follow potato with potato, tomato, eggplant, pepper or tobacco. Rotate with cereals, legumes or grasses for at least 3 years, longer where bacterial wilt is present.

manas.q: Which crops should not come before potato in a rotation?

children.note: Potato has no nursery: the 'nursery' work is choosing healthy seed and preparing it well, plus a deep, clean seedbed.
Plough deep, remove perennial weeds and old potato roots, then open furrows or ridges. Many growers space rows about 75 cm apart with seed 30 cm apart.
Most potato diseases (bacterial wilt, viruses, blight) travel inside seed tubers. Buy certified seed (KEPHIS-certified in Kenya) and renew it every few seasons.

manas.q: What is the main way potato diseases reach a new field?

children.note: A CIP-promoted farmer method: mark the healthiest plants in the field before harvest and keep only their tubers as next season's seed. It cheaply slows disease build-up.

manas.q: What is positive selection in seed potato?

children.note: Medium whole tubers (about egg size) are safest. If large tubers are cut, let pieces heal for a day or two, and never cut seed where bacterial wilt occurs because the knife spreads it.
Spread seed in thin layers under indirect light for a few weeks. Short, green, sturdy sprouts give faster emergence than long pale sprouts from dark stores.
A newer seed technology: rooted cuttings from clean mother plants are sold to seed growers in Kenya and elsewhere to multiply clean seed faster.
Potato is a hungry crop with a short season and a small root system, so nutrients must be available early, close to the seed.
Tubers carry away large amounts of potassium and nitrogen, plus phosphorus, magnesium and sulphur. Potassium is the nutrient removed in the largest amount.

manas.q: Which nutrient do potato tubers remove in the largest amount?

children.note: Place well-decomposed compost or FYM in the furrow at planting and cover it lightly before laying the seed. Placing it close to the roots matters more than spreading it widely.
Fresh manure can burn sprouts, carry weed seed and raise common scab. Use it only on the previous crop or after full composting.

manas.q: Why use mature compost rather than fresh manure for potatoes?

children.note: A legume green manure (e.g. sunn hemp, mucuna, lablab, vetch) dug in a few weeks before planting adds nitrogen and organic matter. Mustard-family covers may also suppress some soil problems.
Use microbes alongside compost, never instead of it.
Dip or sprinkle seed tubers with a slurry of Azotobacter and PSB (and Trichoderma for soil diseases) just before planting, in shade.
Multiply Trichoderma in moist compost for about a week, then place it in the furrow to protect against Rhizoctonia and other soil fungi.
Mycorrhizal fungi help roots take up phosphorus and water; potassium-mobilising bacteria can release some soil potassium. Results vary by soil.
How free-living nitrogen fixers are made, stored and applied.
Phosphate-solubilising bacteria and how to use them.
How mycorrhizal fungi work and how to use them.
At first earthing up, side-dress vermicompost or compost along the row and cover it with the ridge. Wood ash adds potassium but raises pH, so use it lightly.
Pale older leaves suggest nitrogen shortage; scorched leaf edges and dark crinkled leaves suggest potassium shortage; yellow between veins of older leaves suggests magnesium.

manas.q: What leaf sign suggests potassium shortage in potato?

children.note: Steady moisture is the single biggest driver of tuber yield and quality.
Water matters most from tuber initiation (around flowering) through bulking. Stress then means fewer and smaller tubers.

manas.q: When is water most critical for potatoes?

children.note: Swings between dry and wet soil cause growth cracks, knobby tubers and hollow heart. Dry soil at tuber set also favours common scab.

manas.q: Which potato disease is favoured by dry soil at tuber set?

children.note: Furrow or drip keeps leaves dry; sprinkling late in the day keeps leaves wet overnight and invites late blight. Mulch saves moisture on small plots.
Stop irrigating about two weeks before harvest so the skins set and tubers store better.
Most potato pests are managed by clean seed, deep hilling, rotation and quick harvest; biologicals fill the gaps.
Phthorimaea operculella: small grey moth whose larvae mine leaves and tunnel into tubers, in the field and in store. It is a major pest in Kenya and India.
Leaf mines with frass, then tubers with tunnels and droppings near the eyes. Damage climbs fast in storage; in some Indian states storage losses have reached very high levels.

Plant deep, hill well, close soil cracks, harvest promptly and never leave tubers exposed overnight. Use pheromone traps; cover stored tubers with dry repellent leaves (e.g. lantana) or use a granulovirus product where registered.
Rarely cause direct damage on potato but spread potato leafroll virus and PVY, which is why seed crops are grown where aphids are few.

manas.q: Why are aphids important on seed potato crops?

children.note: Soil pests that cut stems or bore holes in tubers. Plough to expose them to birds, avoid planting after grass sod, and use Metarhizium or beneficial nematodes.
Globodera species form tiny cysts on roots and cause patchy, stunted, yellowing crops. It was confirmed in Kenya in the mid-2010s; long rotations, clean seed and not moving soil are key.

manas.q: What does potato cyst nematode do to a field?

children.note: Liriomyza larvae make winding mines in leaves, heavy in dry seasons. Yellow sticky traps and natural parasitoids usually keep it down when broad-spectrum sprays are avoided.
Aphids, whiteflies and thrips in depth.
Cutworms, grubs and wireworms in depth.
Cyst and root-knot nematodes in depth.
Late blight and bacterial wilt are the two biggest disease threats in the tropics; viruses quietly cut yields of recycled seed.
Phytophthora infestans, a water mould that can destroy an unprotected field within about a week of cool, wet weather.
Dark, water-soaked leaf patches with a pale halo and white downy growth underneath in humid mornings; brown stem lesions; reddish-brown dry rot just under the tuber skin.

manas.q: What does late blight look like on the underside of a leaf?

children.note: Tolerant varieties, clean seed, wider spacing, high hilling to shield tubers, and destroying volunteers and cull piles that carry the pathogen between seasons.
Copper sprays are allowed in organic farming within yearly limits; spray before rain as a protectant. Bacillus biocontrol strains show promise in trials but are not yet a full replacement.

links.label: 📄 Source: Plant Pathol J 2021 (Bacillus vs late blight)

children.note: Late and early blight in depth.
Ralstonia solanacearum, a soil and seed-borne bacterium; called brown rot in tubers. No spray cures it.
Plants wilt in the heat of the day and recover at night at first, then wilt for good. Cut tubers show a brown ring and white ooze from the eyes; a cut stem in water streams milky threads.

manas.q: How can you test a potato stem for bacterial wilt?

children.note: Only clean seed and cultural steps work: rotate away from Solanaceae, uproot sick plants with their soil, clean tools and boots, and keep runoff out. Kenya requires lab testing of seed.
Bacterial wilt and other bacterial diseases.
Alternaria solani: brown spots with concentric 'target' rings on older leaves, worse on stressed or underfed plants. Balanced nutrition, rotation and copper or Bacillus sprays help.
Leafroll gives upward-rolled, stiff, pale upper leaves; PVY gives mottling and leaf death. Spread by aphids and seed; manage with clean seed and roguing.
Streptomyces scabies makes rough, corky patches on the tuber skin. Keep soil moist at tuber set and avoid liming and fresh manure.
Rhizoctonia solani: black crusts on tubers that do not wash off and brown cankers on sprouts. Plant into warm soil and use Trichoderma.
Weeds compete most in the first 4–6 weeks before the canopy closes.
Each hilling buries young weeds and protects tubers from greening, moths and blight. Usually done twice.

manas.q: Name two benefits of earthing up potatoes besides weed control.

children.note: Hand hoe before the first hilling; straw mulch works on small plots. Remove couch grass and nightshade weeds that host pests and diseases.
Most quality is lost between the field and the buyer, through bruising, greening and moth damage.
Cut or remove the tops about two weeks before harvest and harvest when the skin no longer rubs off with your thumb.

manas.q: How do you know potato skins are set for harvest?

children.note: Bruises and cuts let rots in. Do not throw bags, and keep harvested tubers out of the sun and rain.
Keep tubers for one to two weeks in a cool, humid, dark, airy place so small wounds heal before storage.
Light turns tubers green, and green parts contain bitter, toxic glycoalkaloids. Store in the dark with good air flow; very cold storage makes tubers sweet and fry dark.

manas.q: Why must ware potatoes be stored in the dark?

children.note: Seed is kept in thin layers on racks in indirect light; this gives short green sprouts and fewer losses than dark heaps.

manas.q: What is a diffused light store used for?

children.note: Tuber moth and other store pests.
Potatoes are mostly sold in local and regional markets, with processing as the growth area.
Kenya's Irish potato regulations require sale by weight in standard bags rather than oversized 'extended' bags; check current county enforcement.
Crisps and chips need high dry matter and low sugar. Choose processing varieties (e.g. Markies, Kufri Chipsona) and avoid very cold storage, which raises sugars.

manas.q: Why do processors avoid potatoes stored very cold?

children.note: KEPHIS inspects and certifies seed in Kenya; in India the seed chain starts from ICAR-CPRI breeder seed, often via tissue culture and minitubers.
Use the East African Organic Products Standard or India's NPOP/PGS-India. Synthetic pesticides and fertilisers are not allowed; copper is allowed with limits.
Supermarkets and processors may test for pesticide residues (MRLs). Organic and low-residue produce can open premium buyers.
Videos from CIP, KALRO, Access Agriculture and gardening educators.
International Potato Center shows how to build a simple seed store with indirect light.
CIP explains how bacterial wilt spreads and the integrated steps that control it.
A short farmer-to-farmer summary of selecting and storing healthy seed.
How rooted cuttings help farmers multiply clean seed potato.
A tour of Kenya's potato research centre and its seed work.
GrowVeg gives practical blight prevention tips for small growers.
Sources for deeper study.
Research, seed systems and training material on potato worldwide.
India's Central Potato Research Institute: varieties and package of practices.
Organic plant health guides for East African crops, including potato.
Biology, ecology and control of potato tuber moth (Potato Research, 2020).
